        caption = "Estimated fixed effects of the final model for healthy fruit weight. Estimates are on the natural log scale, and Ratio is their exponential, which gives the multiplicative change in healthy weight. The reference levels are Control, 2024 and Mullica Queen. The terms marked × 2025 give the additional change in 2025.")
```

### B.5 Sensitivity analysis

To check whether our conclusions depend on the two heated plots with unusually low healthy weight, we removed the `r length(out_pairs)` pairs containing them (`r hw_n_removed` plots, `r round(100 * hw_n_removed / nrow(data), 1)`% of the data) and refitted the final model. The estimated effects became slightly smaller, but all main conclusions were unchanged: the average reduction was `r hw_pct(hw_sub_avg24$ratio)`% in 2024 and `r hw_pct(hw_sub_avg25$ratio)`% in 2025, and the reduction per additional pulse in 2025 was `r hw_pct(hw_sub_slope25$ratio)`%. The only change was that two heat groups in 2024 became individually statistically discernible, which confirms that the evidence for individual heat groups in 2024 is borderline.

### Appendix C: Healthy count: model building (Section 5)

### C.1 Model Specification
```{r, include=FALSE}
# Models to evaluate
m_add_prop <- glmmTMB(cbind(healthy_n, rotten_n) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id), family = betabinomial(link = "logit"), data = data)

m_2way_prop <- glmmTMB(cbind(healthy_n, rotten_n) ~ (heat_group + cultivar + year)^2 + (1 | pair_id), family = betabinomial(link = "logit"), data = data)

m_3way_prop <- glmmTMB(cbind(healthy_n, rotten_n) ~ heat_group * cultivar * year + (1 | pair_id), family = betabinomial(link = "logit"), data = data)
```

```{r}
comparison_anova <- anova(m_add_prop, m_2way_prop, m_3way_prop)

# section below was modified by use of AI chatbot - Gemini
model_comp_prop <- data.frame(
  Outcome = "Healthy berry proportion",
  Model = c(
    "Additive",
    "Two-way interactions",
    "Three-way interactions"
  ),
  df = c(
    attr(logLik(m_add_prop), "df"),
    attr(logLik(m_2way_prop), "df"),
    attr(logLik(m_3way_prop), "df")
  ),
  AIC = c(AIC(m_add_prop), AIC(m_2way_prop), AIC(m_3way_prop)),
  BIC = c(BIC(m_add_prop), BIC(m_2way_prop), BIC(m_3way_prop)),
  LRT_p = c(
    NA,
    comparison_anova$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2],
    comparison_anova$`Pr(>Chisq)`[3]
  )
)

kable(
  model_comp_prop,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Model Comparison for Healthy Berry Proportion"
)

# Winning model: m_add_prop

#We see that the lower AIC value is given by the additive model when the response variable is percentage of healthy berries by count. 

```
From the anova table from above, we can observe that the additive model yeilds the least AIC value whilst still controlling for the complexity. Therefore, m_add_prop was chosen as the model to explain the percentage of healthy fruit by count. 

### C.2 Estimated proportions and comparisons with Control

Table 12 gives the estimated percentage of healthy berries for each heat group, cultivar and year, and Table 13 compares each heat group with Control.
```{r a-hc-predictions}
emm_prop <- emmeans(m_add_prop, ~ heat_group | cultivar * year, type = "response")

contrasts_prop <- contrast(emm_prop, method = "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1, adjust = "dunnett")

predictions_prop <- as.data.frame(emm_prop)
comparisons_prop <- as.data.frame(summary(contrasts_prop, type = "response", infer = TRUE))

predictions_prop %>%
  transmute(Cultivar     = cultivar_labels[as.character(cultivar)],
            Year         = year,
            `Heat group` = group_labels[as.character(heat_group)],
            `Healthy berries, % (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f to %.1f)",
                                                    100 * prob, 100 * asymp.LCL, 100 * asymp.UCL)) %>%
  kable(row.names = FALSE,
        caption = "Estimated percentage of healthy berries by count for each heat group, cultivar and year, from the final beta-binomial model.")

comparisons_prop %>%
  transmute(Cultivar   = cultivar_labels[as.character(cultivar)],
            Year       = year,
            Comparison = paste(group_labels[sub(" / Control", "", as.character(contrast))],
                               "vs Control"),
            `Odds ratio (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)",
                                            odds.ratio, asymp.LCL, asymp.UCL),
            `p-value`  = fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  kable(row.names = FALSE,
        caption = "Odds of a berry being healthy in each heat group relative to Control, from the final beta-binomial model. Intervals and p-values are adjusted for comparing four heat groups with the same Control.")
```


The results from both tables show that heat treatment consistently reduces the proportion of healthy berries count across both cultivars (ST and ST) and both years (2024 and 2025). 

Healthy berry percentages were highest in the unheated Control groups, ranging from 93.9% to 96.0%, while heat-treated groups generally had lower percentages, ranging from 78.7% to 87.2%. 

The odds-ratio comparisons further confirms that all heat treatments significantly reduced the odds of a berry being healthy compared with the Control group (p < 0.001). P-value < 0.001 means there is enough statistical evidence to declare association or difference.  

The odds were approximately 72% lower for the 1, 2, and 3-pulse treatments and 76% lower for the 4-pulse treatment. 

Therefore, we can confidently conclude that the findings suggest that heat exposure negatively affected berry health regardless of cultivar or year.



### Appendix D: Share of healthy fruit by weight: model building (Section 6)

### D.1 Model Selection

```{r, include=FALSE}
data$healthy_weight_prop <- (data$healthy_weight / (data$total_weight))

m1 <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + factor(year) + (1 | pair_id), family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)
m2 <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ (heat_group + cultivar + factor(year))^2 + (1 | pair_id), family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)
m3 <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group * cultivar * factor(year) + (1 | pair_id), family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)

```


```{r}

anova_comp <- anova(m1, m2, m3)
#
## Model Comparison Table
model_comp_tab <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Additive (M_add)", "2-Way Interactions (M_2way)", "3-Way Interactions (M_3way)"),
  df    = c(attr(logLik(m1), "df"), attr(logLik(m2), "df"), attr(logLik(m3), "df")),
  AIC   = c(AIC(m1), AIC(m2), AIC(m3)),
  BIC   = c(BIC(m1), BIC(m2), BIC(m3)),
  LRT_p = c(NA, anova_comp$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2], anova_comp$`Pr(>Chisq)`[3])
)

kable(model_comp_tab, digits = 3, caption = "Model Comparison for Healthy Fruit Percentage by Weight.")

# looks like the winner is m1
```
Table 14 compares the three candidate models. The additive model has the lowest AIC, so it is used to estimate the effect of heat on the percentage of healthy fruit by weight.

### D.2 Model Evaluation

```{r a-hp-coef}
library(dplyr)
library(broom.mixed)
library(knitr)

results <- as.data.frame(summary(m1)$coefficients$cond) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Term") %>%
  filter(grepl("^heat_group", Term)) %>%
  mutate(`Heat group`         = group_labels[sub("heat_group", "", Term)],
         `Odds ratio`         = exp(Estimate),
         `Change in odds (%)` = (exp(Estimate) - 1) * 100,
         `p-value`            = fmt_p(`Pr(>|z|)`)) %>%
  select(`Heat group`, Estimate, `Odds ratio`, `Change in odds (%)`, `p-value`)

kable(results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Heat group effects in the additive beta model for the share of healthy fruit by weight, relative to Control. Estimates are on the logit scale; the odds ratio is their exponential.")
```

We can observe there the effect of heat in the yield of percentage of healthy fruit weight is in the negative direction. This means that the the heat pulses reduces the number yield of proportion of healthy fruit weights.  

```{r a-hp-explore, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3.0, fig.cap="Percentage of healthy fruit by weight for each plot, by heat group, with the mean and one standard error in red. The share is bounded by 0 and 1, which is why a beta model is used."}
ggplot(data, aes(x = heat_group, y = healthy_weight_prop)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey40", size = 1.6) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "red", size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(year ~ cultivar, labeller = labeller(cultivar = cultivar_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Percentage of Healthy fruit by weight") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```


```{r a-hp-candidates, include=FALSE}
hp_fixed <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id),
                    family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)
hp_noyear <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + (1 | pair_id),
                     family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)

hp_year_lrt <- anova(hp_noyear, hp_fixed)
hp_p_year   <- hp_year_lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
```

The beta-binomial model on the counts of healthy and rotten berries is an alternative way to describe the same composition, but it models a share of berries by number, not a share of weight, so its likelihood is not comparable with the beta model. The beta model on the proportion is used for the results in Section 6.

Year contributes little to the share by weight. Dropping it changes the fit by p = `r fmt_p(hp_p_year)`, so the year term is kept only so that this model has the same fixed-effect structure as the other yield models and the measures stay comparable.


```{r,include=FALSE}
weight_predictions <- emmeans(m1, ~ heat_group, type = "response")
print(weight_predictions)
plot(weight_predictions)

coefs <- summary(m1)$coefficients$cond

OR <- exp(coefs[, "Estimate"])

CI <- exp(
  cbind(
    Lower = coefs[, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * coefs[, "Std. Error"],
    Upper = coefs[, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * coefs[, "Std. Error"]
  )
)

results <- data.frame(
  Term = rownames(coefs),
  Odds_Ratio = OR,
  CI_Lower = CI[, "Lower"],
  CI_Upper = CI[, "Upper"],
  p_value = coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

results

healthy_predictions <- emmeans(
  m1,
  ~ heat_group,
  type = "response"
)

healthy_predictions
plot(healthy_predictions)
pairs(healthy_predictions)

```
